summary: Describes Linux Netlink, used both for messaging inside the kernel and between kernel and user space. The focus is Netlink as a protocol between a forwarding engine component and a control plane component. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Inside a computer, one part makes the decisions and another does the work of moving data. Netlink is the way they send messages to each other in Linux. This memo describes it.

questions: netlink protocol forwarding and control plane
subtitle: How Linux kernel and user programs exchange messages about networking.

tldr.problem: Operating systems need a way for the kernel's data forwarding engine and user-space control programs to communicate about how to handle packets and routes. This communication must be structured and extensible to support many different networking services.
tldr.mechanism: Netlink provides a socket-based protocol where user programs connect to kernel services via the PF_NETLINK domain, sending and receiving structured messages with headers, service-specific templates, and Type-Length-Value (TLV) data. Different services (routing, firewall, neighbor discovery) use the same underlying Netlink transport with service-specific message types.
tldr.outcome: Netlink became widely deployed in Linux for managing routing tables, traffic control, interfaces, addresses, and firewall rules, allowing dynamic updates and event notification between control plane and forwarding engine. This design was informational prior art for the IETF ForCES working group.

today: RFC 3549 is Informational and describes Linux Netlink as it existed in kernel 2.4. Netlink remains a core part of Linux networking, used by iproute2 and many other tools to manage routes, interfaces, traffic control, and firewall rules. The design has been extended to additional services beyond those documented here.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Concepts
sections.content:
Linux Netlink evolved from earlier BSD routing sockets to become a general mechanism for separating control (what networking rules to apply) from forwarding (actually moving packets). The RFC focuses on describing Netlink as a protocol between a Forwarding Engine Component (FEC) in the kernel and Control Plane Components (CPCs) in user space.

The core idea is that an IP service is defined by the interaction of these two parts: the FEC processes and forwards packets according to rules, while CPCs (such as routing daemons like OSPF, management tools, or policy enforcement engines) send commands to update those rules. Netlink provides the reliable structured messaging between them, supporting multiple independent services on the same transport.

The RFC documents only the IP service use of Netlink as of kernel 2.4.6, excluding its use for intra-kernel messaging, inter-process communication, or configuration of non-networking services.
sections.plainLanguage: Netlink lets the thinking part of the kernel (control plane) talk to the doing part (forwarding engine) using special messages. Each message type is for a different job, like managing routes or setting up traffic control.

sections.title: Netlink Architecture and Message Format
sections.content:
Netlink logically models FECs and CPCs as nodes on a broadcast wire specific to each service. Nodes register to receive message types of interest, and messages can be unicast, multicast, or broadcast. The service addressing is done via socket creation: a program opens a PF_NETLINK domain socket with a protocol number (such as NETLINK_ROUTE) to connect to that service.

Every Netlink message has three layers. The bottom layer is the Netlink message header (16 bytes) containing the message length, type, flags, sequence number, and process ID. Above that is the IP service specific template—a service-defined structure that varies by service. At the top is service-specific data encoded in TLV (Type-Length-Value) format. The header includes standard flags like NLM_F_REQUEST (this is a request), NLM_F_MULTI (multiple messages follow), and NLM_F_ACK (send an acknowledgment on success).

For GET requests, additional flags like NLM_F_DUMP (return the whole table) and NLM_F_ATOMIC (return a consistent snapshot) allow programs to query the FEC. For NEW requests that modify state, flags like NLM_F_CREATE (create if not present) and NLM_F_REPLACE (overwrite if present) control the behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A Netlink message is like a letter. It has a standard envelope (the header), then the service-specific form you fill out, then the actual data you want to send. The header says whether you want a reply and tracks the message sequence.

sections.title: Header Structure and Error Handling
sections.content:
The Netlink message header is 16 bytes: 4 bytes for total length (including header), 2 bytes for type (standard types like NLMSG_NOOP, NLMSG_ERROR, NLMSG_DONE, or service-defined types), 2 bytes for flags, 4 bytes for sequence number, and 4 bytes for the process ID (PID) of the sender. The sequence number lets the sender match responses to requests, and the PID allows the kernel to multiplex messages to the correct user-space socket.

Error and acknowledgment messages use type NLMSG_ERROR. An error code of zero indicates an ACK (positive acknowledgment); a non-zero error code is a NACK (negative acknowledgment), with the original request data appended so the sender can identify which message failed. Multipart responses are marked with NLM_F_MULTI flag on all but the last message, which has type NLMSG_DONE. A reliable request-response protocol can be built by combining sequence numbers, ACK flags, and timers.

Protocols such as heartbeat monitoring can use the ECHO flag and NLMSG_NOOP messages to detect liveness.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is like an address label and tracking number. It says who sent the message, what kind of message it is, and what response is expected. Errors come back with type NLMSG_ERROR so you know something went wrong.

sections.title: Service Modules and System Services
sections.content:
FE System Services are general utilities accessed via NETLINK_ROUTE even though they are not strictly routing: the network interface service (create, delete, get information about interfaces), the IP address service (add, remove, query addresses on interfaces), and the neighbor table service (manage ARP-like neighbor caches). Each uses its own message template and attributes. For example, the Interface service template contains family (always AF_UNSPEC), device type, interface index, device flags (IFF_UP, IFF_RUNNING, etc.), and a change mask. The IP Address service specifies the address family (AF_INET for IPv4), prefix length, flags for primary vs. secondary addresses, and scope (global, site, link-local, or host-only).

The three main IP services defined in the RFC are NETLINK_ROUTE (routing and related services), NETLINK_FIREWALL (firewall packet redirection and verdicts), and NETLINK_ARPD (neighbor discovery). NETLINK_ROUTE uses message types like RTM_NEWROUTE, RTM_DELROUTE, RTM_GETROUTE for route management, as well as RTM_NEWLINK, RTM_DELLINK, RTM_GETLINK for interface management.

The Route Service Module message template includes the address family, source and destination prefix lengths, type of service (TOS), routing table ID (supporting up to 255 tables), protocol origin (RTPROT_KERNEL for kernel routes, RTPROT_STATIC for administrator-set routes, or higher values for routing daemons), route scope (global, site, link-local, or host-local), and route type (unicast, local, broadcast, anycast, multicast, blackhole, unreachable, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: Netlink organizes different network jobs into services. NETLINK_ROUTE handles routes and interfaces. NETLINK_FIREWALL lets you redirect packets to user space and make accept/drop decisions. NETLINK_ARPD manages the neighbor table. Each service has its own message types and data structures.

sections.title: Traffic Control and Policy Enforcement
sections.content:
The Traffic Control (TC) service allows provisioning of queuing disciplines, classifiers, and traffic shaping rules in a hierarchical manner. A queuing discipline (qdisc) is a scheduler and queue treatment algorithm (FIFO, RED, token bucket, etc.) attached to a network interface. Classes group flows for differential treatment, and filters classify packets to determine which class they belong to. The TC module is accessed through NETLINK_ROUTE with message types RTM_NEWQDISC, RTM_DELQDISC, RTM_GETQDISC (for queuing disciplines), RTM_NEWTCLASS, RTM_DELTCLASS, RTM_GETTCLASS (for classes), and RTM_NEWTFILTER, RTM_DELTFILTER, RTM_GETTFILTER (for filters).

The TC message template contains the interface index, a qdisc handle (typically split into 16-bit major and minor numbers), a parent qdisc handle (for hierarchy), and TCM info (a reference count set by the FE, or priority and protocol fields when used with filters). Generic attributes describe the qdisc type (TCA_KIND, such as 'pfifo' or 'tbf'), statistics (TCA_STATS), rate estimation (TCA_RATE), and service-specific options (TCA_OPTIONS). This design enables Linux to support complex hierarchical traffic management, with multiple queues and scheduling disciplines applied in sequence.

An example given in the RFC shows configuring a simple FIFO queue on an interface, specifying the qdisc type and the limit (number of packets before drops).
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic Control is about deciding which packets get sent first. You can set up nested rules: a parent scheduler divides the link among classes, each class divides its share among subclasses, and filters decide which packets go where. Netlink messages tell the kernel how to set this up.

sections.title: Firewall Service and Packet Verdicts
sections.content:
The NETLINK_FIREWALL service allows user-space programs to receive packets diverted by kernel firewall rules and make policy decisions on them. A firewall rule can be inserted to activate packet redirection. The CPC tells the FEC whether to send just metadata or the full packet data, and optionally the maximum data length. Redirected packets wait in the FEC for a verdict from the CPC.

The mode message from CPC to FEC specifies IPQ_COPY_META (metadata only) or IPQ_COPY_PACKET (full packet), with a range field specifying the maximum number of bytes to copy in the latter case. The packet message from FEC to CPC includes a unique packet ID, a mark value set by the firewall rule, timestamp (seconds and microseconds), hook point (which firewall module it came from), incoming and outgoing interface names, hardware protocol and type, and the packet data payload.

The CPC responds with a verdict message containing the packet ID, the verdict (NF_ACCEPT to let the packet continue or NF_DROP to discard it), and optionally a modified packet payload to be used instead of the original. This allows user-space applications to implement sophisticated firewall policies, content filtering, or other packet interception strategies.
sections.plainLanguage: The firewall service lets user programs see packets that the kernel caught and decide what to do with them. A user program can say 'drop this packet' or 'let it through,' and it can even send back a modified packet.
